     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "245ec3f7-466e-4732-8b36-937e1e6b5c87", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_oxz7Wz22tjRYfAbn1jsauH", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     61	
     62	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     65	
     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     67	
     68	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     69	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     70	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     71	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     72

     94	## Other performance topics
     95	
     96	### Micro-bursting
     97	
     98	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     99	
     100	### Volume initialization after restore
     101	
     102	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized.      104	### Burst credits
     105	
     106	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.

     110	
     111	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     112	2.      5	## Elastic Volumes rules

     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).

     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.

     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.

     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.

     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.

     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.

     2	
     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action.
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     17	
     18	1. Is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?
     19	   - Yes: **Instance**. Say "the volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type". If a volume is also flat at its own limit, report both and fix the instance first, because volume changes cannot deliver above the instance ceiling.
     20	2. Is the instance healthy and one volume flat at its own provisioned limit on the dimension its type is judged by?
     21	   - Yes: **Volume**.
     22	3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume's `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?
     23	   - Yes: **Burst credits**.
     24	4. Did an operation fail on a quota (error text names a limit)?
     25	   - Yes: **Quota**. Use the Capacity and quota headroom section of [review-operational.md](review-operational.md).
     26	5. Are all layers below their limits, latency at the volume's normal level, and queue length low?
     27	   - Yes: **Not EBS**. Check CPU, memory, network and the application.
     28	6. Are all layers below their limits but latency and `VolumeQueueLength` up while IOPS and throughput collapse? This pattern alone does not prove an AWS-side impairment. Check for a direct signal:
     29	   - `VolumeStalledIOCheck` failed (value 1) for the volume, or
     30	   - `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a status check as failed, or
     31	   - an open AWS Health event for the volume, its Availability Zone or its Region.
     32	
     33	   Then decide:
     34	   - A running AWS FIS experiment targets the volume or instance: the latency is injected. Say so plainly; it ends with the experiment (see Step 5 of [troubleshoot-performance.md](troubleshoot-performance.md)). Never recommend more provisioning.
     35	   - One or more direct signals: **AWS-side impairment**. Never recommend more provisioning. Follow the escalation rules below.
     36	   - No direct signal and no FIS experiment: **Indeterminate**. Keep the cause open. Do not name AWS-side impairment and do not recommend more provisioning. Tell the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard for an ongoing AWS-side issue and to watch the volume status checks and `VolumeStalledIOCheck`. If the symptom persists, follow the escalation rules below.
     37	
     38	### Qualitative attribution matrix for "is it storage?"
     39	
     40	From the attribution draft, with the numeric CPU bands removed because no public source states them.
     41	
     42	| CPU | Volume latency | Queue length | Likely attribution |
     43	|---|---|---|---|
     44	| High | High | High | Application drives heavy I/O. Both compute and storage are stressed |
     45	| High | Normal | Low | Compute, not storage |
     46	| Low | High | High | Storage. The application waits on I/O. Go to the decision tree |
     47	| Low | Normal | Low | Neither. Check network, locks and the application |
     48	
     49	"High" and "normal" mean compared with the same resource's own history and the type's documented expectation in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     50	
     51	## Escalation (shared capability)
     52	
     53	Escalate to AWS Support when either is true:
     54	
     55	- Scope signals: an open AWS Health event for the volume, Availability Zone or Region; several resources failing the same way; `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a failing status check.
     56	- A bounded investigation cannot explain the symptom: all layers below limits, no running AWS FIS experiment, no recent change, and the symptom persists.
     57	
     58	Specific cases:
     59	
     60	- Attach or detach stuck: the attachment stays in `attaching` or `detaching` and does not progress. Diagnose (instance state, device name, whether the volume is still mounted, any forced detach already tried), then contact AWS Support.
     61	- Modification in `optimizing` with `Progress` not increasing across several reads, or still optimizing after 24 hours. Tell the user the Amazon EBS User Guide says some performance changes take more than 24 hours, so this is a check, not a fault finding. Escalate with the evidence.
     62	- Snapshot stuck in `pending` with no progress change over the same kind of window.
     63	
     64	Evidence pack to include:
     65	
     66	1. Account placeholder, Region, volume IDs, instance IDs, snapshot IDs as read from the APIs
     67	2. The time window (first ALARM time, symptom start)
     68	3. Metric evidence with units (IOPS, MiB/s, latency, queue length, `EBSIOBalance%`, `BurstBalance`)
     69	4. Volume status and AWS Health results
     70	5. The latest `DescribeVolumesModifications` record per volume, and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events if that optional lookup was available
     71	6. What was ruled out and how
     72	7. The Gaps list
     73	
     74	## Review ratings
     75	
     76	Each review finding has:

     78	| Field | Values |
     79	|---|---|
     80	| Severity | `High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or `Indeterminate` (the data could not be read) |

{"id": "7bee2e253aec4188a06b01b5bd44fcbb", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The slowdown comes from the volume's throughput limit. Starting about 16:17 UTC, the batch job on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (a c6i.xlarge) began large sequential reads (no writes) from gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0, which is attached as /dev/sdg. The volume is set to 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, which is the gp3 baseline. Reads have stayed flat at exactly 125 MiB/s since 16:20. Each read is 256 KiB, so the volume reaches its byte-per-second cap at only about 500 IOPS, which is 17% of the 3000 provisioned. That is why IOPS looks normal while the job slows down. The queue (about 1.5) and read latency (about 3.1 ms per op) are steady, which fits requests being throttled at the cap rather than the volume failing. The instance's own EBS limit is not involved: InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed 0. No volume modification was ever made, so nothing changed on the volume side. The job's read pattern simply needs more than the 125 MiB/s default. Fix: raise the volume's Throughput with ec2 modify-volume, which is an online change with no detach needed. gp3 allows up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS, so at 3000 IOPS you can go up to 750 MiB/s without adding IOPS. The gp3 maximum is 1000 MiB/s, which needs 4000 IOPS or more. You don't need more IOPS. One caveat: a c6i.xlarge has a baseline EBS bandwidth of about 1250 Mbps (~156 MB/s) and can burst to 10 Gbps only for a limited time. If you want much more than about 150 MiB/s sustained across this instance's four volumes, move to a larger instance size too, or the instance limit will bind next.
## Evidence
- Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes went into ALARM at 16:23:18 UTC. Its 1-minute Sum datapoints were 7.8696e9, 7.8680e9 and 7.8696e9 bytes against a 6e9 threshold. 7.87e9 B / 60 s ≈ 131.1 MB/s = 125.0 MiB/s, exactly the provisioned limit.
- ec2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, 20 GiB, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 MiB/s, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 as /dev/sdg.
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadBytes (5-min Sum): 0 before 16:15. From 16:20 to 16:40, every interval is about 39.34e9, a flat 125.07 MiB/s.
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadOps (5-min Sum): about 150,086 per interval, roughly 500 IOPS, far below the 3000 provisioned.
- Average I/O size = 39.34e9 B / 150,086 ops = 262,144 B (256 KiB), so the workload is large sequential reads. VolumeWriteOps/WriteBytes = 0.
- VolumeQueueLength averaged about 1.5 to 1.7. VolumeTotalReadTime is about 466 s per 150k ops, roughly 3.1 ms per read, steady throughout.
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck for i-1234567890abcdef0_3 = 0 every interval from 15:45 to 16:45, so the instance EBS limit is not binding.
- describe_volumes_modifications: no modification has ever been made to the volume.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3
- example-b-gp3-read-bytes
## Gaps
- VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no data for this volume, so the throughput cap is inferred from read bytes sitting exactly at the provisioned 125 MiB/s, not from a direct exceeded-check signal.
- The other volumes on the instance (vol-1234567890abcdef0_19, vol-1234567890abcdef0_4, vol-1234567890abcdef0_15) weren't checked. Their combined load matters for the instance's EBS bandwidth once this volume's throughput is raised.
- The c6i.xlarge EBS bandwidth figures (~1250 Mbps baseline, 10 Gbps burst) come from general knowledge and weren't checked with ec2 describe_instance_types.
- The batch job's own logs and code weren't looked at, so it's unknown why the reads started at about 16:17 or how much data it has left to read.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "f71b8c23-e6cb-4ac7-94a0-e3c7a740fa49", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "I'm ready to wrap up with a final verdict, pinning down the root cause clearly and just once.

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "The bottleneck is the volume's throughput, not its IOPS. vol-0123456789abcdef0 is stuck at exactly its 125 MiB/s throughput limit while using only about 500 of its 3,000 IOPS. Raise the gp3 Throughput setting, not IOPS. You can only raise it to about 141 MiB/s before the c6i.xlarge's own sustained EBS limit takes over, so a real speed-up also needs a larger instance.

**Evidence** (all from this session, times in UTC on 2026-11-23)
- **Volume settings:** gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, attached as /dev/sdg. These are the gp3 defaults, and no modification has ever been recorded for this volume.
- **Alarm:** `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` went to ALARM at 16:23:18. Its datapoints were about 7.87e9 bytes per minute, which is 125.0 MiB/s.
- **Throughput:** 0 before 16:19. From 16:20 to 16:47 it sat flat at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s, all reads.
- **IOPS:** about 500 for the whole window, which is 17% of the 3,000 provisioned.
- **Why IOPS looks normal:** each read is 256 KiB, so the volume hits its byte limit long before its operation limit.
- **The job is waiting on the volume:** queue length held at about 1.5, read latency at about 3.0 ms per operation, and idle time was about 0%. This flat-at-the-limit pattern with steady latency is what a volume capped by its own limit looks like, not a failing one.
- **Not an AWS-side fault:**
  - All four attached volumes report status ok.
  - `VolumeStalledIOCheck` was 0 the whole time.
  - There are no open AWS Health events for EBS or EC2 in us-east-1.
  - Two fault-injection (FIS) latency experiments ran today: one 16:15–16:19, which was stopped, and one running since 16:47. Both target a different volume, vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which is not attached to this instance.

**The instance is not the bottleneck yet, but it is close**

| | Measured, 16:20–16:45 | c6i.xlarge sustained limit (baseline) |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput, all 4 volumes | 132.9 MiB/s | 149.0 MiB/s (156.25 MB/s) |
| IOPS, all 4 volumes | 1,501.5 | 6,000 |

The instance's EBS burst balances (`EBSByteBalance%` and `EBSIOBalance%`) stayed at 99%. Its throughput-exceeded and IOPS-exceeded checks stayed at 0.

**What to change**
1. **Now, online, no detach:** set Throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to **141 MiB/s** and keep 3,000 IOPS. 141 is the instance's 149.0 MiB/s minus what the other volumes use (7.84 MiB/s, almost all from the io2 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_4). That is only about 13% faster.
2. **For a real speed-up:** move to **c6i.2xlarge**, which sustains 298.0 MiB/s and 12,000 IOPS. Then set the volume to about **290 MiB/s**. 3,000 IOPS still covers that, because gp3 allows up to 750 MiB/s at 3,000 IOPS. The instance resize needs a stop/start. c6i.4xlarge sustains 596.0 MiB/s if the job needs more.
3. **Don't** raise IOPS, and don't set the volume much above about 141 MiB/s while it stays on c6i.xlarge. The instance can burst to 1,192 MiB/s, but only until its burst balance runs out. After that it drops back to 149 MiB/s total and the job slows again.

A separate mitigation planner has the sizing above and is drafting the change steps. Any change only runs after operator approval.

**Other things I noticed**
- The io2 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 is also running flat at its 1,000 IOPS limit (7.81 MiB/s). It shares the same instance limit.
- The alarm also fired earlier today, from 07:42 to 07:54 and from 08:03 to 14:00. That suggests the job hits this same ceiling repeatedly.
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 was scaled down today, 08:42–10:49, from 6,000 IOPS / 250 MiB/s to 3,000 / 125. It was idle during the slowdown and doesn't affect it.

**What I couldn't check**
- I didn't search CloudTrail for older volume changes; only the latest modification per volume was checked.
- I didn't look at the batch job's own logs, so I don't know how much throughput it actually wants above 125 MiB/s. Use that number to size the final throughput target.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

## Results
I propose raising the provisioned throughput on gp3 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` from 125 to 141 MiB/s. That's an online change: no detach, no reboot, IOPS stays at 3000. I have not run anything. The plan is for your team to execute, and it passed the safe-deployment policy check on the third try, with no violations left.

**Expect a small gain.** 141 MiB/s is about 13% more read throughput, the most this c6i.xlarge can sustain for this volume (149.01 MiB/s baseline minus about 7.84 MiB/s used by the other volumes). If the job needs much more, see the next step under "What this doesn't cover".

**State I read this session:**
- **Volume** (`vol-0123456789abcdef0`, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1a): gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, in-use on `/dev/sdg` of `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`. No modification has ever been made (`InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound`).
- **Instance** (`i-1234567890abcdef0_3`): c6i.xlarge, running, four attached EBS volumes. The API reports `EbsOptimized=false`, but c6i is EBS-optimized by default, so this doesn't change the sizing.
- **No pipeline step**: the cause is the default limit, not a deployment, so this is a manual change.

## Execution plan (run with your own credentials)

### 1. Prepare: save the current settings for rollback
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
- Record VolumeType=gp3, Size=20, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 as the rollback baseline.
- Stop if any value differs.

### 2. Pre-validate: confirm no modification is in progress
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
- `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or `completed` means go ahead.
- `modifying` or `optimizing` means stop.

Optionally, check that `EBSByteBalance%` for the instance is still high and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` is 0.

### 3. Apply: raise throughput to 141 MiB/s
```bash
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 141
```
- Only the throughput field changes. 141 MiB/s is far below the gp3 cap of 750 MiB/s at 3000 IOPS (0.25 MiB/s per IOPS).
- The state moves `modifying` → `optimizing` → `completed`. The new throughput already applies during `optimizing`.
- **Cost:** a slight increase, for 16 MiB/s of gp3 throughput above the included 125 MiB/s.
- **Modification limit:** this uses one of the 4 allowed modifications per rolling 24 hours. Because no modification has ever been made, this is the first, which leaves 3. A rollback would use another.

### 4. Post-validate: confirm the change took effect
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,Progress:Progress}'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
- Expect TargetThroughput=141, then Throughput=141 and Iops=3000.

Then watch the metrics for 15–30 minutes:
```bash
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes \
  --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 \
  --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 60 \
  --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
```
- **Read throughput:** Sum/60 should rise to about 141 MiB/s (about 8.87e9 bytes per minute), if the job really wants more than 125 MiB/s.
- **Instance check:** `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` should stay 0, and `EBSByteBalance%` should not keep falling.
- **Alarm:** `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` (threshold 6e9 bytes per 60 s) will probably stay in ALARM. Its threshold is below the old 125 MiB/s ceiling, so it is a throughput alarm, not a failure signal.

### 5. Rollback (if needed)
```bash
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
```
- Run it only after the first change reaches `optimizing` or `completed`.
- It counts as a second of the 4 modifications in the 24-hour window.
- IOPS and size don't change, so nothing else needs reverting.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeReadBytes alarm on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** CloudWatch alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes ([redacted ARN]) went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:18 UTC. 3 of 3 one-minute Sum datapoints were above 6.0e9 bytes: 7.8696e9 (16:20), 7.8680e9 (16:21), 7.8696e9 (16:22). The alarm has no actions configured.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:20:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: Batch reads hit vol-0123456789abcdef0's 125 MiB/s gp3 throughput limit
**Description:** gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 ([redacted ARN]) is 20 GiB with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, the gp3 defaults, and has never been modified. Starting 16:20 UTC on 2026-11-23, the batch job on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 has been reading 256 KiB I/Os at a flat 125.04–125.10 MiB/s. That is ~500 IOPS, 17% of the 3,000 provisioned. Queue length holds at ~1.5, latency at ~3.0 ms and idle time at ~0%. This is the pattern of a volume capped by its own throughput limit, not a failing one. Raising the gp3 Throughput setting is the fix; raising IOPS is not.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-read-bytes-alarm

#### Supporting Observations
- **vol-0123456789abcdef0 pinned at 125 MiB/s from 16:20:** Starting 16:19 UTC, this gp3 volume (/dev/sdg) handles reads only. From 16:20 throughput holds flat at ~125.07 MiB/s, which equals its provisioned 125 MiB/s. IOPS stays at ~500 of 3000 provisioned, and the average read size is 256 KiB. Queue length is ~1.5, read latency ~3.0 ms, idle time ~0%, and VolumeStalledIOCheck is 0 throughout. Before 16:19 the volume was idle.
- **Volume and instance configuration:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-b-gp3-throughput) is a 20 GiB gp3 volume with 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput, unencrypted, in us-east-1a. It is attached as /dev/sdg to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (example-perf, c6i.xlarge, EbsOptimized=false, launched 2026-11-23 07:56 UTC). The instance also has vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 (root), vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 and vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 attached. Observed reads of ~7.87e9 B/min (~131 MB/s, ~125 MiB/s) sit flat at the volume's provisioned throughput.
- **All attached volumes healthy:** All four attached volumes report status ok, io-enabled passed and io-performance normal. vol-0123456789abcdef0 has never been modified. AWS Health has no open or upcoming EBS/EC2 events in us-east-1.
- **Instance EBS bandwidth not exhausted:** Instance i-1234567890abcdef0_3 totals ~132.9 MiB/s and ~1,501 IOPS of EBS traffic in 5-minute periods starting 16:20. That is under the c6i.xlarge baseline of 156.25 MB/s and 6,000 IOPS. InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck both stay at 0. EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% stay at 99%, and CPU is ~1.2%. For comparison, the EBS baselines of larger sizes are: c6i.2xlarge 312.5 MB/s / 12k IOPS, c6i.4xlarge 625 MB/s / 20k IOPS, c6i.8xlarge 1250 MB/s / 40k IOPS.
- **FIS experiments target a different volume:** The FIS runs on template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 use action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency, which adds 500 ms latency to 50% of reads and 100% of writes. They target vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which is not attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3. Run EXP1234567890abcdef_4 ran from 16:15:35 to 16:19:24, when a user stopped it. Run EXP1234567890abcdef_7 started at 16:47:04 and is still running. The timing overlaps the read load, but these experiments do not inject latency into vol-0123456789abcdef0. Its ~3 ms latency also matches that. AWS Health shows no open EBS/EC2 events.

#### Gaps
- **Batch job's real throughput demand unknown:** The batch job's own logs were not examined, so it is not known how far above 125 MiB/s the job would read if unthrottled. That number is needed to size the final throughput target.

## Other Gaps

### Older volume changes not checked in CloudTrail

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise the provisioned throughput of gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 MiB/s to 141 MiB/s (IOPS stays 3000, online change).

## Reasoning
The batch job on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) is capped by the volume's default 125 MiB/s throughput: 256 KiB sequential reads at ~500 of 3000 IOPS. 141 MiB/s is the most the instance can sustain for this volume (149.01 MiB/s EBS baseline minus ~7.84 MiB/s used by the other volumes), so expect ~13% gain. A bigger gain needs a c6i.2xlarge resize (stop/start) plus ~290 MiB/s; that is not part of this plan. Passed the safe-deployment policy check; not executed.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Capture the rollback baseline (gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s); stop…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
**Purpose:** Capture the rollback baseline (gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s); stop if any value differs.
**Advisory:** Confirm this saved record is the right rollback baseline for this volume.

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Proceed on NotFound or completed; stop on modifying or optimizing
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Proceed on NotFound or completed; stop on modifying or optimizing.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Raise gp3 throughput to the most the c6i.xlarge baseline can sustain…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 141
```
**Purpose:** Raise gp3 throughput to the most the c6i.xlarge baseline can sustain for this volume.
**Risks:** Slight cost increase for 16 MiB/s above the included 125 MiB/s., Uses 1 of the 4 volume modifications allowed per rolling 24 hours.
**Advisory:** Expected gain is ~13%. A larger sustained gain needs a c6i.2xlarge resize with a stop/start.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the modification reached optimizing or completed with…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,Progress:Progress}' && aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the modification reached optimizing or completed with Throughput=141 and Iops=3000.

#### 4.2 Confirm the job uses the extra throughput without exceeding the…
**Type:** text
Over 15-30 minutes, check that VolumeReadBytes Sum/60 for vol-0123456789abcdef0 rises toward ~141 MiB/s (~8.87e9 bytes/min), and that InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck for i-1234567890abcdef0_3 stays 0 with EBSByteBalance% not steadily falling.
**Purpose:** Confirm the job uses the extra throughput without exceeding the instance EBS limit.
**Advisory:** Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes will likely stay in ALARM; its 6e9 bytes/60 s threshold is below the available throughput., If reads do not rise above 125 MiB/s, the job is not volume-limited.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original throughput, only after the first change reaches…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original throughput, only after the first change reaches optimizing or completed.
**Risks:** Counts as another of the 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24 hours.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the gp3 throughput for vol-0123456789abcdef0 (and the instance size) in infrastructure-as-code.
**Description:** The volume uses the gp3 default of 125 MiB/s, which caps this sequential-read batch job. Set throughput explicitly (141 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge, or ~290 MiB/s with a c6i.2xlarge) in the template defining this volume and instance, sized against the instance EBS baseline minus the other attached volumes, so a redeploy does not reset it.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The IaC definition declares gp3 Throughput >= 141 MiB/s and Iops 3000 for this volume.
- Total provisioned throughput of all attached volumes does not exceed the instance type's EBS baseline in MiB/s.
- A redeploy does not reset the volume throughput to 125 MiB/s.

     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.

     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.

     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.

     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.

{"id": "bba7de4e-dc88-4b24-8659-76f4d1095329", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_P96nTZZ94vhaVigLTvIayM", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: Elastic Volumes modification
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", "how long will optimizing take?"
     6	- A `ModifyVolume` call failed with an error.
     7	- Sizing a resize, an IOPS or throughput change, or a gp2 to gp3 migration.
     8	- Extending the file system after a size increase.
     9	- Shrinking a volume or cancelling a modification.
     10	
     11	## Procedure
     12	
     13	1. **Find the volume.** Use the volume ID the user gives, or discover it with `DescribeVolumes` (by instance attachment or by the volumes that have recent modifications). Never pick a volume by its Name tag alone; confirm the ID with the user if more than one matches.
     14	2. **Read the latest modification record.** `DescribeVolumesModifications` for the volume: `ModificationState`, `Progress`, original and target values (size, type, IOPS, throughput), `StartTime`, `EndTime`, `StatusMessage`. This API returns only the most recent modification request for each volume. Use it for the current or latest modification state, not for history.
     15	3. **Answer the asked question first, in plain words.**
     16	   - `modifying` or `optimizing`: not stuck. In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies and performance is between the source and the target. It completes on its own.
     17	   - `completed`: done. The new values apply.
     18	   - `failed`: read `StatusMessage` and translate it (step 5).
     19	   - Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     20	4. **Count the modifications in the rolling 24 hours.** Up to 4 per volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. `DescribeVolumesModifications` cannot give this count, because it returns only the latest modification. Count the `ModifyVolume` events for the volume in the last 24 hours with the optional AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` call (filter on the volume ID as the resource name, or on the event name `ModifyVolume`). Report how many remain in the current window. As a cross-check, the latest record from step 2 should appear among those events if its `StartTime` is in the last 24 hours. If the lookup is denied or unavailable, record a Gap ("the number of modifications in the last 24 hours could not be confirmed") and do not state how many remain.
     21	5. **Translate errors.**
     22	   - io2 "Iops to volume size ratio of ... is too high; maximum is 1000": io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB. To reach the target IOPS, the size must be at least target IOPS / 1,000 GiB. Propose that size together with the IOPS.
     23	   - gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS. If a request breaks either rule, give the size or IOPS that satisfies it.
     24	   - Size decrease: not allowed. Size can only increase. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     25	   - Cancel: a submitted modification cannot be cancelled. Wait for it to complete; a reverse change then counts toward the 4 in 24 hours.
     26	   - Limit reached: the 4 modifications in the window are used. The next one is possible when the oldest falls out of the rolling 24-hour window.
     27	   - Older instance types or MBR volumes: check the Elastic Volumes requirements page.
     28	6. **Size a new target.**
     29	   - Keep it within the instance's remaining EBS baseline: `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline (converted to MiB/s) minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     30	   - gp2 to gp3: keep at least the gp2 volume's current baseline IOPS (3 x GiB, minimum 100) and its measured throughput. gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size; provision more only if measured demand needs it.
     31	   - State how the target was computed.
     32	7. **File system extension after a size increase.** Give the commands for the operator to run on the instance. Never execute them.
     33	   - `lsblk` to see the device and partition
     34	   - `sudo growpart /dev/<device> <partition-number>` if the volume has a partition
     35	   - `sudo xfs_growfs -d <mount-point>` for XFS, or `sudo resize2fs /dev/<device-or-partition>` for ext4
     36	   - Point to the extend-the-file-system guide for Windows and other cases.
     37	8. **Separate findings.** If the instance caps what the volume can deliver, write that under Separate findings. Never phrase it as "the modification failed" when the record shows `optimizing` or `completed`.
     38	
     39	## Decision rules
     40	
     41	- The modification record decides the Answer. Performance metrics never override it.
     42	- An instance ceiling is a Separate finding with its own recommendation (instance type change).
     43	- Use the binding-layer tree in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) only when the user also asks about performance.
     44	
     45	## What to report
     46	
     47	The verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). The Answer names the state and what it means. Evidence lists the record fields. Recommendation gives the exact next call, if any. Gaps list anything unreadable.
     48	
     49	## Safety rules
     50	
     51	- The agent never runs `ModifyVolume` on its own. It proposes it as a directed action, approved on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     52	- The proposal includes: the exact call (`--volume-id`, and only the changed fields among `--size`, `--volume-type`, `--iops`, `--throughput`), the expected state sequence (`modifying`, `optimizing`, `completed`), how many of the 4 modifications in the rolling 24 hours remain after this change (only when step 4 confirmed the count; otherwise say it is unconfirmed), cost direction, and rollback.
     53	- Rollback: after the change completes, a reverse change of IOPS, throughput or type is possible and counts toward the 4. Size cannot roll back.
     54	- Recommend a snapshot before a type change or a large resize on a volume with data the user cannot lose.
     55	
     56	## Sources
     57	
     58	- Modify a volume: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modify-volume.html
     59	- January 2026 What's New post: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/01/amazon-ebs-up-to-four-volume-modifications/
     60	- Monitoring modifications: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/monitoring-volume-modifications.html

     63	- Modification duration (1 TiB, about six hours, more than 24 hours): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modify-volume.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/monitoring-volume-modifications.html
     64	- Requirements: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/modify-volume-requirements.html
     65	- Extend the file system: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/recognize-expanded-volume-linux.html
     66	- gp3 and gp2: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html
     67	- io2: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html
     68	- Amazon EBS-optimized instances: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ebs-optimized.html"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_qfRMYnze64PWy48cKooyfv", "content": [{"text": "{"012345678901_1": "AWS API error (ec2.describe_volumes_modifications, account 012345678901_1): InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound \u2014 Modification for volume 'vol-0123456789abcdef0' does not exist."}"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

That's an online change: no detach, no reboot, IOPS stays at 3000. I have not run anything. The plan is for your team to execute, and it passed the safe-deployment policy check on the third try, with no violations left.

**Expect a small gain.** 141 MiB/s is about 13% more read throughput, the most this c6i.xlarge can sustain for this volume (149.01 MiB/s baseline minus about 7.84 MiB/s used by the other volumes). If the job needs much more, see the next step under "What this doesn't cover".

**State I read this session:**
- **Volume** (`vol-0123456789abcdef0`, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1a): gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, in-use on `/dev/sdg` of `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`. No modification has ever been made (`InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound`).
- **Instance** (`i-1234567890abcdef0_3`): c6i.xlarge, running, four attached EBS volumes. The API reports `EbsOptimized=false`, but c6i is EBS-optimized by default, so this doesn't change the sizing.
- **No pipeline step**: the cause is the default limit, not a deployment, so this is a manual change.

## Execution plan (run with your own credentials)

### 1. Prepare: save the current settings for rollback
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
- Record VolumeType=gp3, Size=20, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 as the rollback baseline.
- Stop if any value differs.

### 2. Pre-validate: confirm no modification is in progress
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
- `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or `completed` means go ahead.
- `modifying` or `optimizing` means stop.

Optionally, check that `EBSByteBalance%` for the instance is still high and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` is 0.

### 3. Apply: raise throughput to 141 MiB/s
```bash
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 141
```
- Only the throughput field changes. 141 MiB/s is far below the gp3 cap of 750 MiB/s at 3000 IOPS (0.25 MiB/s per IOPS).
- The state moves `modifying` → `optimizing` → `completed`. The new throughput already applies during `optimizing`.
- **Cost:** a slight increase, for 16 MiB/s of gp3 throughput above the included 125 MiB/s.
- **Modification limit:** this uses one of the 4 allowed modifications per rolling 24 hours. Because no modification has ever been made, this is the first, which leaves 3. A rollback would use another.

### 4. Post-validate: confirm the change took effect
```bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,Progress:Progress}'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
- Expect TargetThroughput=141, then Throughput=141 and Iops=3000.

Then watch the metrics for 15–30 minutes:
```bash
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes \
  --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 \
  --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 60 \
  --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
```
- **Read throughput:** Sum/60 should rise to about 141 MiB/s (about 8.87e9 bytes per minute), if the job really wants more than 125 MiB/s.
- **Instance check:** `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` should stay 0, and `EBSByteBalance%` should not keep falling.
- **Alarm:** `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` (threshold 6e9 bytes per 60 s) will probably stay in ALARM. Its threshold is below the old 125 MiB/s ceiling, so it is a throughput alarm, not a failure signal.

### 5. Rollback (if needed)
```bash
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
```
- Run it only after the first change reaches `optimizing` or `completed`.
- It counts as a second of the 4 modifications in the 24-hour window.
- IOPS and size don't change, so nothing else needs reverting.

## What this doesn't cover
- **Bigger sustained gain:** resize the instance to c6i.2xlarge (298.0 MiB/s and 12,000 IOPS baseline), then set this volume to about 290 MiB/s at 3000 IOPS (298.0 − 7.84 rounded down). The resize needs a stop/start and therefore downtime, so it should be scheduled. It also costs more for the instance and uses a second volume modification. I did not run it through the policy check.
- **Don't go above about 141 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge.** It would only last while the instance's burst balance holds, then fall back to the baseline.
- **Unconfirmed demand:** we don't know if the job really needs more than 125 MiB/s, because its app logs weren't available. Step 4 answers that: if reads don't rise above 125 MiB/s, the job isn't limited by the volume.
- **Unrelated, deliberately left alone:** the running FIS experiment `EXP1234567890abcdef_7` targets `vol-1234567890abcdef0_11`, which isn't attached to this instance.
